headline: Pooling United, Delta and American shows a revenue response to a fuel cost shock but does not pin down its size: a year later unit revenue has made up between 49% and 104% of the cost (90% range; 68 carrier-quarters from 31 distinct quarters, worth about 16 independent ones).
plain_summary: Pooling United, Delta and American shows a revenue response to a fuel cost shock but does not pin down its size: a year later unit revenue has made up between 49% and 104% of the cost (90% range; 68 carrier-quarters from 31 distinct quarters, worth about 16 independent ones).
The 68 rows come from 31 distinct quarters in 8 calendar years; because all carriers face the same fuel price, they count for about 16 independent quarters.
Least-squares estimate: 85% after a year and 85% in the long run, half of that within 0.7 quarters (90% range 0.3 to 13.5; the speed is not pinned down).
United alone, as published: 75% after a year (49% to 91%). Pooled: 85% (49% to 104%).
The pooled 90% range is 29% wider than United's (55 against 43 points).
Like for like (United refitted here on the same resamples): the pooled range is 10% wider.
United alone: 75% after a year (49% to 99%, 30 quarters).
Delta alone: 177% after a year (-157% to 494%, 12 quarters, which cannot be told from no response).
American alone: 78% after a year (38% to 105%, 26 quarters).
No gap between two carriers is distinguishable from zero.
Variant with 2022-2023 added back and a traveller-growth control: 143% after a year (77% to 182%, 92 rows).
Out of sample United (10 quarters from 2024): average miss 0.55 cents per ASM for the pooled curve, 0.66 for no response, 0.57 for full immediate recovery, 0.56 for management's path.
Out of sample Delta (11 quarters from 2024): average miss 0.63 cents per ASM for the pooled curve, 0.88 for no response, 0.47 for full immediate recovery, 0.54 for management's path.
Out of sample American (10 quarters from 2024): average miss 0.53 cents per ASM for the pooled curve, 0.86 for no response, 0.57 for full immediate recovery, 0.48 for management's path.
That comparison was chosen after the United-only test on the same years had been seen.
Co-movement, not proof of cause: fuel prices and travel demand move together.

definition.recovery: recovery(k) = L x (1 - rho^(k+1)): the share of a lasting fuel cost change that unit revenue has made up k quarters after the shock. L is the long-run share, rho the part of the remaining gap left open each quarter, half-life ln(0.5)/ln(rho) quarters.
definition.equation: d4(revenue per ASM)[i,t] = a[i] + L * sum_{j=0..4} (1 - rho) rho^j * d4(fuel cost per ASM)[i,t-j] + c * capacity growth[i,t] + e[i,t]; i a carrier, a[i] its intercept, all in cents per available seat mile, capacity growth in percent year over year
definition.measures: Revenue over ASM and fuel expense over ASM from data/lab/peer_quarterly.csv. United's fare clock uses the unit revenue printed in the release and price per gallon times gallons, which agree with these to rounding.
definition.pandemic_rule: A row is dropped when any level from 8 quarters back to the quarter itself lies in 2020Q1-2021Q4: the fare clock's rule.
definition.estimation: Least squares: rho on the fare clock's grid from 0 to 0.95 in steps of 0.01, L in closed form given rho.
definition.uncertainty: Moving-block bootstrap over calendar quarters: blocks of 4 consecutive distinct quarters, with every carrier's row for a drawn quarter kept together, L and rho re-estimated on each resample. Ranges are percentiles of the resamples; curve_draws are the resampled curves. Rows of one quarter are never treated as independent. The clean quarters are not contiguous (2019Q4 is followed by 2024Q1), so a block can straddle the gap.
definition.n_quarters_effective: Rows divided by the design effect, capped at the number of distinct quarters. The design effect is the squared ratio of the 90% range of the one-year share under the quarter-block bootstrap to the same range when single rows are resampled as if independent.

lag_regression.interval: 90% Student t with (quarters - 1) degrees of freedom on the largest of the three errors
lag_regression.note: The unrestricted five-lag regression on the same rows, with carrier intercepts: running sums of the lag coefficients, with classical errors, errors clustered by quarter, and clustered errors with four quarters of serial correlation. lo and hi use the largest.

by_carrier.method: Each carrier's own two-parameter curve (its own intercept and capacity coefficient), fitted on the same quarter resamples as the pooled curve so the gaps between carriers respect the common fuel shock. A resample with fewer than 8 rows for a carrier is not fitted for that carrier. Gaps are differences in the one-year share with p05 to p95 ranges.

variant_with_2022.label: VARIANT, not the headline: the 2022-2023 quarters, which the main estimate drops because 2020-2021 levels sit behind their year-over-year changes, are added back with a demand control.
variant_with_2022.controls: Year-over-year growth in TSA checkpoint travellers (percent) for quarters from 2022Q1 on, and an indicator for those quarters: the traveller series starts in 2019, so it has no year-over-year figure for 2015-2019 and the indicator keeps the missing figures from acting as zeros. Carrier intercepts and capacity growth as in the main estimate.
variant_with_2022.caveat: The added quarters compare 2022 with 2021 and carry lagged fuel changes measured against 2020: the rebound from the pandemic and the 2022 fuel spike happened together, and one national traveller count cannot fully separate them.

oos.definition: Predicted year-over-year change in revenue per ASM (cents) under each rule, given the fuel cost per ASM and capacity that actually occurred: a constant and a capacity coefficient common to all carriers, estimated on the quarters before 2024 with the rule's fuel response held fixed, plus the rule's fuel term. One constant, not one per carrier, because Delta has a single usable quarter before the cut. mae is the mean absolute error in cents per ASM over n carrier-quarters; the fuel-term-only figures drop the baseline.
oos.management_path_note: 0.45 in the quarter of the shock, 0.85 one quarter later, 1.0 afterwards, as specified for this comparison.
oos.note: This specification (the two-parameter curve, pooled over carriers) was chosen AFTER the United-only test on these same years had been seen. The scores are descriptive, not a clean test.

united_only_refitted_here.note: United alone from the tracked panel (revenue over ASM and reported fuel expense over ASM), on the same quarter resamples as the pooled curve: the like-for-like comparison.

limits: Co-movement, not causation: fuel prices and travel demand rise and fall together with the economy, so part of any measured response is demand and not airlines passing on cost. Pooling carriers adds rows, not new fuel shocks: every carrier sees the same fuel price in the same quarter.

Scope differs between carriers. United: consolidated revenue, fuel expense and capacity from its earnings releases. Delta: the adjusted total revenue (third-party refinery sales removed) and adjusted fuel expense printed in its releases, not the GAAP figures. American: consolidated revenue and fuel from SEC XBRL facts over mainline capacity from BTS traffic filings.

American's capacity base is narrower than its revenue: BTS seat miles are for the American (and, to mid-2015, US Airways) operating certificates and leave out regional partners and some international flying, while revenue and fuel are consolidated. Its cents-per-ASM figures are therefore too high in level; the recovery share is a ratio of two such figures and is distorted only as far as the mainline share of capacity moves.

American's fuel figure covers mainline flying only before 2020 (as first filed) and all flying from 2020 (later filings restate the line to a higher figure, which matches regional fuel having been moved into it). The earlier figures are multiplied by one factor, the fiscal 2019 fuel expense as restated over the same year as first filed, which assumes the regional share of fuel was constant from 2014 to 2019. The estimate without that factor is listed under variants_tried.
American enters from 2014Q1, the first full quarter after its merger with US Airways, so its first usable row is 2016Q1.

Delta owns a refinery. Its adjusted figures remove third-party refinery sales, but the refinery still changes the fuel price Delta pays relative to the market, so its fuel shock is not the same shock as the others'.
Delta's adjusted figures start in 2018, so it contributes one quarter before 2020 and the rest from 2024: it adds almost nothing to the earlier period and its own curve rests on very few quarters.

Hedging in the early years: reported fuel expense includes the results of fuel hedges, so the fuel cost a carrier reported after the 2014 fall in oil prices did not move one for one with the market price, and not by the same amount at each carrier. Hedge results are not separated here.
The clean sample is 2015-2019 and 2024 onwards; the largest fuel spike before 2026 (2022) is outside it and enters only in the labelled variant.

Year-over-year changes overlap by three quarters. The bootstrap uses blocks of four quarters, which with about thirty distinct quarters means roughly eight independent blocks; the ranges are probably still too narrow.
L (the long-run share) and rho (the speed) trade off against each other; the one-year share is the better determined quantity and the half-life the weaker one.

american_fuel_as_first_filed.description: As the main estimate with American's pre-2020 fuel as first filed (mainline only, no scope factor)

without_american.description: As the main estimate without American (release-based carriers only)

variants_tried: pooled_smooth_carrier_intercepts_capacity_clean_quarters: the main estimate (two-parameter curve, carrier intercepts, capacity control, pandemic-touched quarters dropped, American's pre-2020 fuel brought to consolidated scope).
pooled_five_lag_regression_same_rows: the unrestricted five-lag regression with quarter-clustered errors (pooled.lag_regression).
american_fuel_as_first_filed: As the main estimate with American's pre-2020 fuel as first filed (mainline only, no scope factor).
without_american: As the main estimate without American (release-based carriers only).
variant_with_2022: 2022-2023 quarters added back with TSA traveller growth and an indicator for quarters from 2022 (variant_with_2022), and the same rows without the traveller control.
per_carrier_smooth: each carrier's own two-parameter curve on the shared quarter resamples (by_carrier).
oos_pre_2024: the pooled curve fitted on quarters before 2024 and scored on 2024 onwards (oos); chosen after the United-only test had been seen.
